e.t: Abiel is a proper name, rendered “Abiēl” or “Avil.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs four times, in four verses: twice in 1 Samuel, once in 2 Samuel, and once in 1 Chronicles. The name appears in passages that identify individuals, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain each person’s particular role. Its normal meaning here is therefore the personal name Abiel, with Avil given as another rendering.

This word means “container”: an object used to hold or carry something. As a noun, it refers broadly to a vessel or receptacle rather than to one particular kind of object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 22 times across 20 verses, including passages involving supplies, ritual liquids, and other stored contents. Its use ranges across several books, so the surrounding passage identifies what kind of container is intended in a given verse.

This adjective describes someone who is headstrong—firmly determined to follow their own will rather than readily accept guidance or correction. It presents a person as difficult to turn or persuade, emphasizing stubborn self-direction. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in Sirach. Its basic sense is therefore a characterization of a person’s resistant, self-willed disposition, while the surrounding verse determines the specific situation in which that quality is being described.

This word means “its doorpost,” referring to the upright side support of a doorway. It is a noun naming a specific architectural part, with “its” showing that the doorpost belongs to or is associated with something already mentioned. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs ten times, all in Ezekiel 40, where the description repeatedly measures and identifies parts of the temple’s entrances. Its meaning remains concrete and structural rather than referring to a person, action, or abstract idea.

This Greek LXX verb means to “sharpen” or “whet”—to make something sharp. It describes an action rather than an object, person, or quality. The central idea is increasing sharpness, especially by working on an edge or point. This word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament represented by the LXX data, appearing in Psalms and Proverbs. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains the action of sharpening.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person called Aliel or Alil. It is not presented as an ordinary descriptive word, action, or quality, so its basic function is to identify an individual rather than express a general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:47. Without the verse text or a broader passage, no further meaning or personal significance should be assigned to the name itself.

This verb means “break camp” or “return to,” describing movement away from a place or the resumption of travel. It can refer to a group moving on after staying somewhere, or to someone turning back toward a destination. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, it occurs 11 times. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on whether the surrounding passage emphasizes departure, movement, or returning.

This verb means to fill someone with courage—to strengthen a person inwardly so that courage is present. It describes an action rather than simply naming courage itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 15:23. The reference identifies its only recorded occurrence, while the word’s basic meaning remains “fill with courage.” Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Annan is a personal name used to identify an individual in the Greek Old Testament text. The available lexical information gives “Annan” as the name itself, without providing an additional meaning or description. In this LXX corpus, the name occurs three times, all in 1 Samuel: 1 Samuel 1:5, 1:19, and 2:21. Its role is therefore primarily identifying a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or theological concept.

This adjective describes someone or something as “irresponsible.” It presents conduct or character negatively, identifying a lack of responsibility rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs seven times across seven verses: once in Ezekiel and six times in deuterocanonical writings. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means to denounce or contradict. It describes speaking against someone, rejecting what has been said, or openly opposing a claim. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs eight times in the Greek LXX corpus, across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on whether the surrounding passage emphasizes refusal, accusation, or disagreement.

This verb means “not hope”: it expresses the absence of hope or the act of not hoping. It is found five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, appearing in Esther, Isaiah, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains a negative expression concerning hope.

This verb means “bind”: to fasten, tie, or hold something so it is not free to move. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 33:8. The precise force of the action depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains fastening or restraining something. This word should be kept distinct from other Greek words that may also be translated with English expressions related to binding.

This verb means “fail in hitting”—to miss the intended target rather than strike it. It describes an unsuccessful attempt and focuses on the result: the person does not hit what was aimed at. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 31:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the failure to hit or reach the intended mark.

Aptalim is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once in the Greek LXX text, in Joshua 16:3, and is rendered “Aptalim.” The available wording identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whether it refers to a person, place, family, or another named entity. Its precise referent therefore belongs to the context of Joshua 16:3 rather than to the name’s basic lexical meaning.

This Greek word means “bread” or “loaves,” referring to food made from grain and eaten as ordinary nourishment. It is a noun used throughout the Greek Old Testament, including references to daily food and loaves used in worship. The word occurs 283 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scriptures of this corpus, so its central meaning is broad and familiar rather than rare or specialized. The surrounding passage determines whether it refers to bread generally or to particular loaves.

This verb means to mis-aim or miss the mark. It describes failing to reach the intended target, whether through poor direction or an unsuccessful attempt. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Sirach. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. Its central idea is straightforward: the aim falls short of what was intended. The surrounding verse is needed to determine what specific target or goal is in view in either occurrence.

This Greek LXX noun means “exemption,” referring to release from an obligation, requirement, or burden. It names a condition in which someone or something is not required to meet a stated demand. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 10:34. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea is being excused or freed from a requirement.

This noun means “taking away; carrying off.” It refers to the removal or taking of something from one place, person, or possession. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, so its basic sense is clear even though no verse text is available for explaining its particular use. The word functions as a noun naming the act or result of taking something away.

This adverb means “abundantly” or “ungrudgingly,” describing an action done generously, freely, or without reluctance. It can indicate that something is given or carried out in a plentiful manner rather than sparingly or resentfully. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 7:13. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its central idea is generous abundance offered without reservation.

Achiōr, also rendered Akhior, is a personal name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Numbers 34:27, identifying an individual. Because it functions as a proper name, its ordinary meaning is the person it names, not a broader concept that can be defined in English. The supplied lexical information gives the name’s forms but does not provide a separate word-definition or etymological sense.

Bamael, also rendered Vamel, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament and appears once, at 1 Chronicles 7:33. Because the name itself is not defined as a descriptive term, its meaning is best understood as the personal designation Bamael or Vamel, while the surrounding verse identifies whom it names.

This noun means “hole”: an opening or hollow in the ground or another surface. It identifies a physical place or depression rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, it occurs 22 times, so its basic sense appears across several books and settings. The surrounding verse determines what kind of hole is intended. It may be described or located, but the word itself names the hole.

Gethremmōn, also rendered Yethremmon, is a proper name rather than a common word with a stated descriptive meaning. It identifies the same named entity wherever it appears in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs twice in this corpus, once in Joshua 19:45 and once in 1 Chronicles 6:54. Since the available information gives the name but no explanation of its underlying meaning, it is best understood as a name preserved by transliteration rather than translated into an ordinary English term.

Gesem, also rendered Yesem, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is therefore its designation of someone or something named Gesem or Yesem; the name itself is not given a further definition here. This word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis and Exodus, and its earliest recorded occurrence is Genesis 45:10. Its precise referent in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “old age,” referring to the advanced stage of life rather than youth. It describes a person’s later years and can be used when speaking about growing old or reaching life’s end. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs 39 times, so it is a recurring term for age and life’s later season. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

“Nakedness” refers to the condition of being without clothing or adequate covering. This Greek LXX noun names that state rather than describing an action. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament translation, in Deuteronomy 28:48. The word’s basic sense is therefore straightforward: exposed bodily condition or the absence of covering. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

Darōm is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament, rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. Its role is to identify the named entity represented by this name; the available lexical record does not provide an additional ordinary meaning. It occurs once in the LXX, at Ezekiel 21:2. The surrounding verse text must determine what the name identifies in that passage.

This verb means “scatter”: to cause people or things to spread apart rather than remain together. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes separation or dispersal and may be used for groups, individuals, or objects. It occurs 44 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, so its basic sense is well established across many passages. The surrounding verse determines whether the scattering is physical or refers more broadly to people being dispersed. Its lexical meaning is an action—something or someone is scattered.

This word means “justly”: it describes an action done in a right and just manner. As an adverb, it tells how someone acts, judges, speaks, or carries out a responsibility. It is used twelve times in the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented in this corpus, including passages from Genesis, Deuteronomy, Proverbs, Wisdom, and Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the action and surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains the manner of acting justly.

This adverb describes acting in a treacherous or crafty way—using deceit, hidden intent, or cunning rather than openness. It tells how someone performs an action, emphasizing the deceptive manner of that action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 9:3; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its precise force there. Its basic sense remains conduct marked by craftiness or treachery.

This adjective describes something as “of ill omen” or “boding”—something viewed as warning of trouble or an unfavorable outcome. It functions as a descriptive word, marking a person, sign, report, or circumstance as carrying a threatening or ominous indication. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject being described.

This pronoun means “of himself” or “his own,” pointing back to a person already mentioned or marking something as belonging to that person. It can therefore express self-reference or possession, depending on how it functions in a sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 3,947 times, so its basic role appears across many kinds of statements rather than describing one particular subject or event. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding words.

This adjective describes something that is “containing fruit.” It functions as a descriptive word, identifying a thing by what it holds or contains rather than naming the fruit itself. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it appears once, at Jeremiah 38:12. The word’s basic meaning is therefore specific and limited: it points to something characterized by the presence of fruit. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This interjection expresses a strong wish or longing, meaning “would that!” It introduces something the speaker desires to happen or be true. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, including once in Job and three times in the Deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what follows, but its central sense remains an earnest expression of desire.

This adjective means “each individually,” pointing to members of a group one by one rather than treating them only as a whole. It can describe separate persons, objects, or actions, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 12 times, including several uses in Ezekiel and 2 Maccabees. Its basic force is distributive: attention is given to every member separately. The surrounding verse determines exactly which people or things are being considered individually.

gl: force a besieged town to surrender
d: force a besieged town to surrender

e.t: It is a verb meaning “force a besieged town to surrender.” It describes the sustained action of surrounding or attacking a fortified place until its defenders give up. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears twice, both times in Joshua, so its usual sense is specifically connected with military siege rather than a general kind of pressure or persuasion. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context.

This verb means “defiled”: made unclean, polluted, or morally corrupted. It describes an action rather than a person or object by itself—the subject causes something to become defiled. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 3:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the bringing of defilement or uncleanness. The word therefore points to a condition produced by an act of contamination or violation.

Eliada is a proper name for a person. The name is also given as “Eliatha.” In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs twice, referring to named individuals in genealogical or historical lists rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in 1 Chronicles 3:8 and once in 2 Chronicles 17:17. As a personal name, its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and the person being identified.

This Greek LXX verb means that something is “in” or “contents,” indicating presence within something else. It can describe what is located inside, what a thing contains, or what exists within a person or place. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings, including passages from Exodus, Kings, Job, Proverbs, and Maccabees. Its exact English wording depends on what is being described in the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means to “dwell in” or “inhabit”—to live within a place or among a people. It describes settled residence rather than merely passing through. The word appears 34 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, especially in Isaiah and Jeremiah, where it commonly refers to living in a land or place. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “six thousand.” It is an adjective used with a number or group to express a quantity of six thousand people, objects, or other counted things. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it appears nine times, including passages in Numbers, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, and 2 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains numerical: it identifies the size of a group or amount rather than describing a quality, action, or spiritual idea.

This verb means “come out” or “go out.” It describes movement from one place, position, or setting to another, with attention to leaving or emerging. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it appears 631 times, so it is a broadly used action word rather than a rare expression. The exact English wording may depend on whether the sentence emphasizes coming outward or going away, but the central idea remains departure or emergence.

This Greek LXX verb means “promise”: to state that one will give, do, or uphold something. It describes a pledged commitment rather than merely mentioning a future possibility. The word appears 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including Proverbs, Esther, and the Maccabean writings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains the act of promising or pledging something.

This noun means “hearkening” and “obedience”: attentive listening expressed through a willing response. It describes more than merely hearing words; it points to receiving what is said in a way that leads to obedience. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Samuel 15:22, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains clear: listening that honors the instruction received by responding obediently.

This verb means “annoy”: it describes an action that annoys another person. It is used as a verb, so it expresses what someone does rather than naming a person or thing. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, all in deuterocanonical books—twice in 2 Maccabees and once in 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to cover something or put something over it. It describes the act of placing a covering across or above another thing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Lamentations 3:43–44. The word itself expresses an action, while the surrounding passage determines what is being covered and why. Its central idea remains straightforward: to cover, to spread something over, or to place it above another object.

Eselia is a proper name, referring to a particular person or place rather than expressing a general quality, action, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 34:8. Because it is a name and no broader definition is provided, its meaning is best understood as identifying the named subject in that passage. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly whom or what Eselia identifies there.

This Greek LXX adjective means “last” or “farthest part.” It describes something at the end of a sequence, period, or area, or at the most distant point. The word can therefore express either final position or distance, depending on what it describes. It occurs 141 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing regular use for both temporal and spatial senses. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This adjective describes someone who is good-hearted and open-hearted—personable, sincere, and free from a suspicious or calculating attitude. It points to an inward disposition rather than an outward action, so the word characterizes the kind of heart a person has. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 2:32; the surrounding verse is needed to explain its particular force there.

This verb means “straighten” or “steer”: it describes making something follow a direct course or guiding it in a chosen direction. Its basic idea concerns directing movement rather than merely observing or describing it. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, including both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being directed and on the surrounding sentence.

This noun means “courage” or “boldness”—the inner strength and confidence to act without shrinking back. It describes a quality of brave resolve rather than a physical object or action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 13:18. The word’s exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is a willingness to face difficulty with confidence and determination.

Ἡλιόδωρος is a proper name, referring to a particular man rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears 13 times in the Greek LXX corpus, all in 2 Maccabees, from 2 Maccabees 3:7 through 5:18. The name is also represented as “Hēliodōros” and “Iliothoros.” Its exact significance in any individual verse must be understood from that verse’s surrounding passage.

Ēsamathim, also rendered Isamathim, is a proper name—the identifying name of a person or family line rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 2:53. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide its surrounding verse text or a further explanation of the person, its significance must be understood from the genealogy and context of that passage.

This noun means “incense,” referring to fragrant material burned or presented in worship. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 74 times, chiefly in passages concerning Israel’s worship and offerings. The word appears often in Numbers and Exodus, and it also occurs in Leviticus, Chronicles, Samuel, Genesis, and 2 Maccabees. Its central idea remains the incense itself rather than the act of burning it. The surrounding passage determines whether the reference concerns preparation, offering, handling, or another use of incense.

Iebasam, also rendered Ievasam, is a personal name rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 7:2. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is chiefly its identification of a particular person in the biblical record, not a general concept to apply elsewhere. The surrounding verse is needed to identify that person’s specific place in the genealogy.

Iemeni is a proper name referring to a person named Iemeni. As a name, it identifies someone rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The Greek LXX form appears five times, in Judges, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, and Psalms. The supplied references identify its occurrences, but without the surrounding verse text they do not establish further details about the person or the significance of each appearance.

Iothor is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship, so it is normally understood as a personal name rather than translated for its meaning. The name occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing especially in Exodus and also in Judges, Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. Its specific connection to people in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means “make equal,” describing an action that brings something into equality or the same standing. It expresses the act of making things correspond rather than merely comparing them. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in the books of Job and Psalms. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic idea remains the same: to make equal.

Issari is a proper name preserved as “Issari.” It identifies a named individual or family designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this name occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles: 24:22 and 26:29. Since no verse text is included here, the name’s particular role in each listing must be understood from its surrounding passage.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “pierce through” or “stab.” It describes an action that penetrates something with force, rather than merely touching or marking its surface. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Jeremiah and once in Ezekiel, so its normal sense is focused and concrete. The exact force intended in either verse is clarified by its surrounding passage, but the central idea remains piercing or stabbing through something.

This Greek LXX verb means “prevail over”: to overcome or gain the upper hand against someone or something. It describes the result of one side becoming stronger or more successful than another. The word appears 28 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, so its basic idea applies across several accounts and passages. The exact force in any particular verse depends on what conflict, opposition, or situation the surrounding text describes.

This verb means to “nest” or “camp”: to settle down, make a dwelling, or remain in a place. It can describe the act of taking up residence, whether for people or for creatures. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 53 times, showing a recurring idea of dwelling or settling rather than a single isolated use. The precise force in any verse depends on what or who is said to settle and the surrounding passage.

This word means “pot,” referring to a container made for holding something. It is a noun, so it names the vessel itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Isaiah and Jeremiah. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: a physical pot or similar container, while the surrounding verse determines what is placed in it or why it is mentioned.

This Greek LXX noun means “ashes,” referring to the powdery remains associated with something burned. It names a physical substance rather than an action or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX material represented here, both times in 3 Maccabees. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains the same: ashes.

This noun means “creation”: what has been made or brought into being. It can refer broadly to the created order rather than to one particular object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs 10 times across 10 verses, showing that it is a recurring term for the created world or the act and result of making. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains creation as something brought into existence.

Leia, also rendered Lia, is a personal name rather than a descriptive word. It identifies a woman in the Greek Old Testament and functions as a proper name wherever it appears. The name occurs 28 times in the LXX, with most occurrences in Genesis and a few later appearances in Ruth and Proverbs. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding text, but the word itself serves simply to name Leia or Lia.

This verb means “become leprous,” describing the onset or condition of a serious skin disease. It focuses on a person coming to have leprosy rather than merely naming the disease itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in 2 Kings, including references to Naaman and King Uzziah. The exact force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is the transition into being leprous or becoming afflicted with leprosy.

This word means a cook: a person whose role is to prepare food. It is a noun, naming the worker rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 8:13. Its basic meaning is straightforward and practical, identifying someone responsible for cooking. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the word’s particular role in that passage.

This Greek noun means “prophesying” or “prophetic power”—the activity or capacity associated with prophecy. It refers to prophetic expression as a recognizable kind of power or practice, rather than naming a person. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 15 times, including passages in Numbers, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and other books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains connected with prophesying and prophetic power.

Masemannē, also rendered Masemanni, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person or named figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs once in the Greek text, at 1 Chronicles 12:11. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its identity and role need the surrounding context for a fuller description.

This noun means a warrior or fighter—someone identified by readiness or ability to engage in battle. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for people associated with fighting strength rather than for an action itself. The word occurs 22 times across 21 verses, with occurrences in books such as Judges, Samuel, Chronicles, Jeremiah, Joel, and Zechariah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and whether the person is being described as a combatant or as part of a group of fighting men.

This LXX noun refers to someone registered in a genealogy. It identifies a person whose name or family record has been entered in a genealogical listing. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Ezra 2:62. Its basic sense is therefore connected with formal inclusion in a recorded family line, rather than with a general list or ordinary personal description.

This noun means “care; attention”—the focused concern or thoughtful regard given to something. It describes mental or personal attention rather than a specific action, so it can refer to giving careful consideration, remaining attentive, or taking something seriously. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 14 times, appearing especially in Psalms and also in Job, Ecclesiastes, and Lamentations. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on what the surrounding sentence says receives this care or attention.

This verb means to “change a man's persuasion”—to alter what a man has been persuaded to believe or accept. It describes an active change in another person’s conviction rather than simply presenting an argument. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 11:25. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the changing of a man’s persuasion.

This noun means “thigh,” the upper part of the leg between the hip and knee. In the Greek Old Testament, it names a physical part of the body rather than an action, quality, or spiritual concept. It occurs six times, all in six Old Testament verses, with five occurrences in Leviticus and one in Job. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding text.

This word is a proper name identified as “Myndos; Minthos.” It functions as the name of a specific person, place, or other named entity rather than as a general description, though the available information does not specify which kind of entity it names. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 15:23. The verse reference identifies its location, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the name’s particular role there.

“Nabouthai” or “Navuthe” is a proper name, not a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs 19 times in 17 verses, appearing in 1 Kings and 2 Kings. Because the available information gives the name’s form and references but no verse text or additional definition, its significance in any particular passage must be understood from that passage’s surrounding context.

Odom, also rendered Othom, is a proper name identifying a person. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 31:15. Because it is a personal name rather than a common noun or descriptive word, its basic meaning is the individual it names. The available information identifies the name and its single occurrence but does not provide additional details about the person or explain the surrounding verse.

This word means “compassion”: a tender concern that moves someone to care about another person’s distress. It describes the feeling or quality of mercy shown toward those who need help, relief, or forgiveness. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 27 times, so it is a recurring expression for compassionate care rather than a rare or highly specialized idea. Its exact force in a particular verse is shaped by the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “eye,” referring to the organ of sight. It is a noun used for the physical eye or eyes, and its ordinary meaning remains straightforward across its LXX usage. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, appearing in Proverbs, Wisdom, and 4 Maccabees. Because the surrounding verse text is not included, its precise figurative or contextual force in any particular passage cannot be stated here; the basic word itself denotes an eye.

This verb means to cut something upright or to do it correctly. It expresses the idea of making a straight, accurate course rather than acting crookedly or carelessly. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Proverbs, so its recorded use is limited to that book and should be understood according to the surrounding sentence. As a verb, it describes an action: directing, shaping, or carrying something out in a straight and proper way.

Oudouia is a proper name, also rendered “Uthoia,” rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or group in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available information does not establish which without the verse text. This name occurs once, at Nehemiah 7:43, and its precise referent must be identified from that passage’s context.

This verb means “disguise”: to conceal or alter someone’s appearance or identity so that the person is not recognized as they truly are. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Isaiah 44:8 and Ezekiel 22:26. Those references establish its limited use in this corpus, while the word’s basic meaning remains the act of disguising. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person or thing being described.

“Hewn” describes something cut, shaped, or carved from a larger material, usually by means of a tool. It is an adjective, so it identifies an object by the way it was prepared rather than naming the action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at 1 Kings 10:22. Its basic sense is therefore a material that has been deliberately shaped through cutting or carving.

This word means “errant,” describing someone or something that has gone astray or wanders from the proper path. It can function as an adjective, describing a person or thing as straying, and also as a noun referring to one who is errant. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Job and once in Jeremiah. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea remains being misguided, wandering, or out of the right way.

This verb means to “exert oneself” or “busy oneself.” It describes actively applying one’s effort to work, activity, or responsibilities rather than remaining inactive. The word appears once in the Greek Septuagint, in 1 Kings 10:22, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic idea is purposeful activity: a person occupies himself with something and gives effort to it.

This Greek LXX noun means “penalty” or “fine”—a payment or imposed consequence required because of an offense or violation. It names a form of judgment rather than an action, person, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament translation, in 2 Maccabees 7:36. Its precise force in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is an imposed penalty or financial charge.

Raabias, also rendered Rhaavias, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, object, or quality. It identifies a particular person in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 26:25. Since no verse text or surrounding passage is available here, the name’s precise role in that passage cannot be described further; its basic meaning is the personal name itself.

This word means “that which flows” or “flow,” referring to something moving continuously like a stream or current. It is a noun, so it names the flowing substance or movement rather than describing an action. In the Greek of the Septuagint’s deuterocanonical books, it occurs once, in Sirach 39:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains something that pours, runs, or moves onward. The word therefore presents flow as a recognizable thing or stream of movement.

Sadouch, also rendered Sathukh, is a proper name referring to a person. It is not a general description or action word, but a name used to identify someone. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Kings 4:4. The available wording identifies the name itself, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the person’s specific role there.

This word means “trumpet,” a noun referring to a wind instrument used to produce a clear, carrying sound. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears in passages involving public announcements, assembled worship, procession, battle signals, and other occasions when a sound needed to be heard by many people. It occurs 89 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including the deuterocanonical books. Its basic meaning remains the instrument itself; the surrounding passage determines whether the trumpet’s use marks gathering, celebration, warning, or another public signal.

Sedekia, also rendered Sethekia, is a proper name used for people in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies individuals rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs nine times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, appearing once in 2 Kings, once in 1 Chronicles, and seven times in Jeremiah. Because it is a personal name, the surrounding passage is needed to determine which individual is meant in a particular verse.

Selcha is a proper name, also given as “Selkha.” It identifies a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX, the name occurs five times across five Old Testament verses, including passages in Deuteronomy, Joshua, 1 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. Its exact referent in any particular verse must be determined from that verse’s surrounding text.

This word means “spittle,” referring to saliva released from the mouth. It is a noun naming a physical substance, not an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 40:15. The word’s basic meaning is straightforward, while its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the verse uses the image. It should therefore be understood simply as a term for spittle or saliva within its single recorded occurrence.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “darkness,” referring to a condition in which light is absent or hidden. As a noun, it names that condition rather than an action. In the LXX corpus, it occurs three times, and each occurrence is rendered “darkness.” Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the state or presence of darkness.

This proper noun refers to the Spartans, the people of Sparta. It is a name for a particular nation or community rather than a general description of someone’s character or conduct. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, the word occurs nine times, all in 1 Maccabees, across eight verses. The supplied references place it in letters and historical notices involving the Spartans, but the word itself identifies the people. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun refers to suet, the thick animal fat, and can also mean dough. Its central sense is a tangible substance rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs 92 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek deuterocanonical material, with especially frequent use in Leviticus, where sacrificial and dietary descriptions make bodily fat an important reference. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the basic meaning remains suet or dough.

This word means “robe,” referring to a garment worn as clothing. It is a noun naming the item itself, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 89 times, so it can describe clothing in a range of passages, including accounts involving families, worship, priestly service, and other settings. Its central idea remains simple: a robe or substantial garment worn by a person. The precise significance of the robe in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means “weep with”: to share another person’s tears or sorrow rather than remain emotionally distant. It describes joining someone in grief, expressing fellow-feeling through mourning. The word appears six times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical text, including Psalms, Isaiah, Lamentations, and Sirach. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is grieving alongside others. It is an action word that portrays compassionate participation in another person’s distress.

This verb means “come with; come together.” It describes joining another person or group, or arriving together with others. The emphasis is on people coming into shared company or association. It occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is consistent across several settings. The surrounding verse determines who is joining whom and why, but the word itself expresses coming together or accompanying others.

This noun means “dwelling in one tent,” describing shared residence under the same tent. It refers to living together in one tent rather than naming a person or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Exodus 16:16. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s exact force in that occurrence must be understood from its context.

Titos is a proper name identifying a person called Titos. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 11:34. Because the available information gives the name but not the verse text or surrounding context, it does not establish further details about who Titos was or what role he had. The name itself simply identifies him.

“Hardihood” means boldness or daring, especially the quality of acting with unusual courage or nerve. As a noun, it names a person’s bold disposition rather than an action itself. In the Greek LXX material represented here, the word occurs twice, both in Sirach, so its meaning is focused rather than broadly repeated across many biblical books. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine whether that boldness is being praised, questioned, or warned against in either passage.

This adjective describes someone or something given to wantonness—behavior marked by little restraint and self-indulgence. It expresses a quality of reckless conduct rather than a neutral description of desire. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Proverbs 20:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense points to wanton conduct and an undisciplined character.

d: light shewing through a small hole: a narrow opening

e.t: This noun refers to light showing through a small hole, or to a narrow opening itself. It describes a limited passage through which light can appear, rather than a broad window or open space. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 41:16. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is a small opening associated with light passing through it.

φιλοφρόνως means “amicably”: it describes speaking or acting in a friendly, peaceable way toward someone. As an adverb, it tells how an action is carried out rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense describes conduct marked by goodwill and courteous friendliness, while the surrounding verse determines the precise action it describes.

This Greek noun means a plant, referring to vegetation that grows or is planted. It is used 17 times in the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented in this corpus. Its wording can describe a plant generally, or vegetation viewed as established in the ground. The term appears in passages from Genesis, Kings, Job, and Ezekiel, showing ordinary use for living growth rather than an abstract idea.

This noun means “light”—illumination that makes things visible and distinguishes brightness from darkness. It can refer to light as a created reality, as shown at the opening of Genesis, and it is used broadly throughout the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. The word occurs 154 times in the Greek LXX corpus, so its basic meaning is well established across many kinds of passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.
